content.title: About
content.content: Gin is a distilled spirit made from grain alcohol flavored with juniper berries and a variety of other botanicals. It has a distinctive piney aroma and is a staple base for many classic cocktails.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “gin” derives from the English “juniper,” the primary botanical used for flavoring.
The first gin, known as “genever,” originated in the Netherlands in the 17th century before becoming popular in England.
Classic London Dry Gin contains no sugar after distillation, giving it a dry, clean taste.
There are over 100 styles of gin, each differing in the blend of botanicals.
Gin is a key ingredient in cocktails such as the Martini, Gimlet, and Tom Collins.

items.title: Antioxidant properties of juniper
items.content: Juniper essential oils contain antioxidants that may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Botanicals like coriander and angelica traditionally support digestion and relieve bloating.

items.title: Stress reduction
items.content: Moderate consumption can promote relaxation thanks to aromatic compounds.

items.title: Alcohol intoxication
items.content: Gin typically has a high alcohol content (40 % ABV or higher), so it should be enjoyed in moderation.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of sedatives and certain antibiotics.

items.title: Allergy to botanicals
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to juniper or other herbs used in gin.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Gin is often served chilled neat, but most commonly it is mixed in cocktails. The classic “gin & tonic” with a lime wedge is a popular choice. Gin can also be added to marinades, sauces, or desserts for a botanical twist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bottle in a cool, dark place with the cap tightly sealed. Properly stored gin retains its flavor profile for many years.

content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger is a hot sandwich consisting of a beef patty placed between a split bun, often accompanied by cheese, lettuce, tomato, onion, sauces and seasonings. In school cafeterias of 1698 it was prepared from simple, locally available ingredients and served as a hearty meal for students.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first school hamburger appeared in 1698 in a historic school cafeteria, where it was prepared by student‑cooks.
The traditional bun was lightly toasted over an open fire, and the patty was cooked on a cast‑iron griddle.
The original recipe used only pure beef, without any soy or plant‑based fillers.
Hamburgers were often served with sauerkraut instead of modern sauces.
In some schools, melted cottage cheese was used in place of cheese, as it was more readily available.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburgers supply B12, B6 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein, fat and carbohydrates in the bun offers sustained satiety and quick energy.

items.title: Provides fiber
items.content: When topped with lettuce, tomato and onion, the sandwich adds dietary fiber beneficial for digestion.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: The patty and cheese can contain significant saturated fat, which may increase cardiovascular risk if consumed frequently.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Historical recipes often relied on salt and dried spices for flavor, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, posing a risk for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogenic bacteria, so the patty should be cooked thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten with the hands, holding the bun. They can be topped with mustard, ketchup or a homemade sauce. Optional additions include fresh lettuce, tomato slices, onion, and a slice of cheese that melts over the hot patty.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A freshly prepared hamburger is best consumed immediately. For storage, separate the components: keep the cooked patty refrigerated for up to 2 days, the bun in a dry paper bag, and the vegetables in an airtight container. Reheat the patty thoroughly before assembling.

content.title: About
content.content: Hayacas are a traditional Puerto Rican bread roll made from wheat flour, sugar, butter, eggs, and yeast. The dough is slightly sweet, soft, and airy, with a golden crust on the outside. Hayacas are commonly served for breakfast, lunch, or as a snack, and can be paired with cheese, ham, or sweet fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hayacas appeared in Puerto Rico in the early 20th century under American culinary influence.
Traditionally the rolls are baked as small round buns, but they are also shaped into “pancakes” for special occasions.
The original recipe uses milk, giving the crumb a more tender texture than ordinary bread.
Hayacas are often served with “avocado mash” or a sweet cinnamon‑sugar glaze called “moco”.
Puerto Rico celebrates “Hayaca Day”, when hundreds of rolls are baked for charitable events.

items.title: Carbohydrate source
items.content: Hayacas provide a quick source of energy thanks to their mix of simple and complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs and milk in the recipe add a modest amount of complete protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour and yeast are rich in B1, B2, and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Milk and butter supply calcium and phosphorus, important for bone health.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Traditional recipes use salt sparingly, making the roll suitable for moderate sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Hayacas contain wheat flour and are not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Added sugar makes the product calorie‑dense; those monitoring blood sugar should limit portions.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: Milk and butter may cause issues for individuals with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of butter and sugar, the roll is relatively high in calories; moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hayacas can be eaten fresh, lightly toasted, with butter, jam, cheese, or ham. They are often sliced in half and used as sandwich bases. In sweet versions, the rolls are drizzled with cinnamon‑sugar glaze.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store hayacas in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator (up to 7 days) or freeze in a sealed bag for up to 3 months. Warm in the oven or toaster before serving.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-home-recip.title: Pasta with Tomato-Based Sauce, Home Recipe

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with tomato sauce is a classic Italian dish made from boiled pasta and a sauce based on ripe tomatoes, olive oil, garlic, and aromatic herbs. It is simple, nutritious, and flavorful, suitable for everyday meals or special occasions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce first appeared in Italy in the 19th century when tomatoes became widely available.
Traditional Italian pasta is often cooked "al dente" to retain a firm bite.
The combination of tomatoes and basil is the classic "marinara" sauce, one of the most popular pasta sauces.
Early pasta was made from durum wheat, giving it a higher protein content than soft wheat pasta.
Different regions of Italy pair specific pasta shapes (spaghetti, penne, fettuccine) with particular sauces.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that may support heart health and reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Provides complex carbohydrates
items.content: Durum wheat pasta offers slow‑releasing energy, helping to keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Source of vitamin C and potassium
items.content: Tomatoes are high in vitamin C and potassium, important for immune function and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain pasta increases fiber content, which benefits digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with a modest amount of olive oil, the dish remains light and heart‑friendly.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten, so people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding pre‑made tomato sauce or excessive salt can make the dish high in sodium, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Acidity of tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes may aggravate acid reflux in individuals with gastritis or heartburn.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Boil pasta in salted water until al dente. In a skillet, heat olive oil, sauté minced garlic, then add fresh or canned tomatoes, basil, oregano, salt, and pepper. Simmer 10‑15 minutes, then toss with the cooked pasta, mix well, and serve topped with grated Parmesan if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The sauce can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Cooked pasta is best used immediately, but can be kept in cold water in the fridge for up to 24 hours to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Quinoa is the seed of the plant Chenopodium quinoa, native to the Andes. It is a pseudocereal rich in protein, fiber, and micronutrients. The “no added fat” version is a dry product without added oils, ready for cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quinoa was a staple food of the Incas and was called the “mother of all grains”.
There are more than 120 varieties of quinoa, differing in seed color: white, red, and black.
Quinoa is naturally gluten‑free, making it suitable for gluten‑free diets.
The seeds contain all nine essential amino acids, providing a complete protein source.
Unlike most grains, quinoa contains notable amounts of mono‑ and polyunsaturated fats, but the no‑added‑fat version keeps them minimal.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: About 14 % of dry quinoa weight is protein, which helps maintain muscle mass and promotes satiety.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and promotes a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of magnesium and iron
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while iron is essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Quinoa contains quercetin and kaempferol, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Consuming quinoa leads to a gradual rise in blood glucose, beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Saponin content
items.content: Saponins can cause mild stomach irritation in sensitive individuals; rinsing quinoa before cooking is recommended.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Although rare, some people may experience an allergy to quinoa.

items.title: High oxalate levels
items.content: Those prone to kidney stones should limit quinoa intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook quinoa in a 1:2 ratio of grain to water for 15‑20 minutes until the seeds become tender and the germ separates. It can be added to salads, soups, side dishes, used as a base for vegetarian patties, or substituted for rice in many recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry quinoa in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: The Light Vegetable Dip is a smooth sauce made from fresh vegetables, low‑fat yogurt, and aromatic herbs. It has a mild, slightly tangy flavor and low calorie density, making it an ideal choice for diet‑friendly eating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dip is prepared without butter or sour cream, reducing saturated fat content.
It contains carrots, cucumbers, bell pepper and green onion, providing a broad range of vitamins and minerals.
The recipe is inspired by Mediterranean cuisine, where similar sauces are commonly served with fresh vegetable appetizers.
Light dip is often used as a salad dressing instead of richer sauces.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The vegetables supply vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: One tablespoon (≈30 g) provides about 25 kcal, convenient for weight control.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: The yogurt base contains probiotics that help maintain a healthy gut flora.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: No added salt makes it suitable for blood‑pressure management.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The yogurt may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Fresh vegetable content
items.content: Improper storage can lead to rapid spoilage, increasing the risk of foodborne illness.

items.title: Nitrate content
items.content: High nitrate levels in vegetables may be undesirable when consumed in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve with fresh vegetable sticks, whole‑grain crackers, use as a salad dressing, or as a sauce for baked meats. It can be gently warmed, but is best kept cold to preserve texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in a sealed container for up to 5 days. Discard if a sour odor or discoloration appears.
